headline: CodeMiko Teleports a Physical Chair Into Her Virtual World
lede: Youna Kang, the VTuber known as CodeMiko, has demonstrated a new level of physical-to-digital integration: she 3D-scanned a real chair and brought it into her virtual performance space, where she can grab, touch, and move it with convincing fidelity. The test, built inside Unreal Engine, showed no hand-clipping or floating — the persistent failure mode that makes prop interaction look cheap. She described it as a proof that she could "teleport" any physical object into her digital world.
body:
Most *VTubers* — performers who animate a digital avatar in real time using motion capture — operate in a largely empty virtual stage. Props, when they exist at all, are static decorations that the character's hands notoriously fail to interact with convincingly. CodeMiko has built her reputation on closing that gap. The chair demonstration is her most concrete step yet toward a live performance environment where physical and digital objects coexist on the same terms.

The workflow she demonstrated combines two technologies: *3D scanning*, which converts a real-world object into a polygon mesh by photographing it from many angles, and real-time physics and inverse kinematics inside Unreal Engine, which govern how a digital hand actually contacts and grips that mesh. Getting both halves to agree — so that the avatar's fingers neither sink through the surface nor hover above it — is genuinely hard. The Unreal Engine editor visible in the clip shows the chair registered as an interactive actor inside her persistent stage environment, meaning it persists across sessions rather than being re-imported each time.

The significance extends beyond a single piece of furniture. If the pipeline is repeatable, Kang could in principle scan any object from her physical workspace — a coffee cup, a keyboard, a prop weapon — and have it behave as a tangible object inside her broadcast. That collapses a boundary that live VTubing has never managed to close, and it suggests a near-future in which a performer's physical and virtual environments are simply mirrors of each other.

Kang's technical ambition is already well-documented in the 3D-art press. The publication 80.lv noted that her **hair simulation** — a separate system — already behaves like real hair inside Unreal Engine, something few VTubers have matched. The chair test adds interactive prop physics to that list. None of this is commercially available tooling aimed at hobbyists; it reflects sustained investment in a custom pipeline that most independent creators cannot replicate.

concepts.definition: Short for Virtual YouTuber: a content creator who performs as a real-time animated digital avatar, typically driven by motion-capture hardware that maps the performer's body movements onto the character. Originating in Japan around 2016, the format has grown into a global industry.

Technology that records the movement of a person or object and translates it into digital animation data. In VTubing, this typically involves tracking suits, headsets, or camera-based systems that feed skeletal position data into a game engine in real time.

A process that captures the shape of a physical object and converts it into a three-dimensional digital mesh. Common methods include photogrammetry (using many photographs) and structured-light or LiDAR scanning. The resulting mesh can be imported into game engines or animation tools.

A mathematical technique used in animation and robotics to determine how a chain of joints (like an arm) must be positioned so that its endpoint (like a hand) reaches a target point in space. In VTubing, IK is what makes a character's hand appear to actually touch a surface rather than float above or clip through it.
